Part 1 · The blanket of air
01What the air is made ofFig. 3.2 · composition of the atmosphere35 XP

Here is the air around you as a hundred squares. Two gases take ninety-nine of them. Tap each gas to find its own — and look closely at the one square that is left.

—

The Earth's atmosphere is a mixture of gases. Nitrogen and oxygen are the two primary and most abundant, and both are essential to life. Carbon dioxide, argon, helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone and hydrogen are also present, but in far smaller quantities.

Besides these the atmosphere carries water vapour and tiny dust particles. The amount of water vapour varies, generally between 0.1 and 0.4 per cent, and it plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation. The composition of the atmosphere also varies with altitude.

Think about it
The atmosphere is pulled down around the Earth by gravity. It shields us from harmful radiation coming from the Sun, including ultraviolet, and it regulates the Earth's temperature by trapping some of the Sun's energy instead of letting it all escape to space. Can you imagine what would happen if there were no atmosphere at all?
02Straight up through five layersFig. 3.3 · structure of the atmosphere35 XP

Climb from the ground to the edge of space. The layers are marked out by one thing only: what the temperature does as you rise.

Layer
—
Temperature
—
What is here
—

The layers are defined by changes in temperature and density with increasing altitude. The density of air is highest near the Earth's surface and decreases with height. Each boundary has its own name: the tropopause between troposphere and stratosphere, the stratopause below the mesosphere, and the mesopause above it.

The troposphere averages about 12 km and holds the air we breathe, most of the water vapour and the clouds — nearly all weather happens here. The stratosphere reaches 50 km, is free of cloud and weather disturbance, and carries the ozone layer. The mesosphere reaches 80 km, where most meteorites burn up. The thermosphere runs from 80 to 700 km, reflects radio waves, contains the ionosphere and hosts the auroras. Above it the exosphere is so thin that helium and hydrogen simply float away into space.

Don't miss out
Temperature decreases with altitude only in the troposphere and the mesosphere. In the stratosphere and the thermosphere it rises — in the thermosphere very rapidly indeed, because the gas molecules there absorb the Sun's X-rays and short-wave ultraviolet.
03Which layer does this happen in?One clue each, and no repeats30 XP

Every one of these belongs to exactly one layer. Work out which from what you have just climbed through.

The word aurora comes from Latin, meaning dawn or morning light, and is named after the Roman goddess of dawn. The solar wind — charged particles emitted by the Sun — is directed towards the magnetic poles on reaching the Earth's atmosphere, and as those particles meet different atmospheric gases each gas glows with its own colour. The display is called the Aurora Borealis in the Northern Hemisphere and the Aurora Australis in the Southern.

04Weather, or climate?A day, against thirty years25 XP

They are not the same word for the same thing. One is what today is doing; the other is what a place is like. Mark each statement.

Weather refers to the hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions of the atmosphere, and it can vary significantly from one day to the next. Climate is the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for an extended period — usually thirty years or more.

The elements that shape both are the same five: temperature, humidity, precipitation, atmospheric pressure and wind. Temperature is governed largely by insolation, the incoming solar energy the Earth intercepts, which decreases from the equator towards the poles — and so the temperature does too.

A word to know
Humidity is the presence of water vapour in the air. As air gets warmer its capacity to hold water vapour increases, so humidity rises — which is why on a humid day clothes take longer to dry and sweat evaporates slowly, leaving you uncomfortable. Precipitation happens when part of the atmosphere becomes saturated with water vapour, which condenses and falls under gravity: drizzle, rain, snow, sleet and hail.
Part 2 · Pressure, and the wind it makes
05High pressure, low pressureWhere every wind comes from35 XP

Warm the ground and the air above it does one thing; cool it and the air does the opposite. Everything else in this chapter follows from that.

The air is
—
Surface pressure
—
Sky
—

The pressure exerted by the weight of air on the Earth's surface is called air pressure. It is highest at sea level and falls rapidly with altitude. Horizontally, it is decided by temperature: where it is hot the air heats, expands and rises, creating a low-pressure area, which brings cloudy skies and wet weather. Where it is cold the air is heavy and sinks, creating a high-pressure area, which brings clear and sunny skies.

Air always moves from high-pressure areas to low-pressure areas, and that movement is wind. Winds are named after the direction they blow from — a wind blowing from the west is a westerly.

Don't miss out
The air above us presses on our bodies with real force, and yet we never feel it. That is because air presses on us from every side at once, and our bodies exert an equal counter-pressure outward — the two cancel.
06Sea breeze and land breezeFig. 3.8 · the same rule, twice a day30 XP

Land and sea do not heat or cool at the same rate, and the coast feels the difference every single day. Switch between noon and midnight.

Which is warmer
—
The wind blows
—
—

The sea breeze is a local wind that blows from sea to land during the day, especially in the afternoon, when the land becomes relatively warmer than the sea. That forms a low-pressure region over the land, so the wind starts blowing in off the water.

The land breeze blows from land to sea at night, because land cools faster than sea. Since the difference in temperature and pressure between sea and land is small at night, the land breeze is the weaker of the two. Together they are essential in creating the moderate climatic conditions of coastal regions.

Wind is simply the movement of air from a high-pressure area to a low-pressure area, and it can be gentle or strong. You can watch it blow dry leaves down a pavement, lift dust — or uproot trees in a storm.

Part 3 · India's seasons, and the monsoon
08The four seasons the IMD countsPut the year in order25 XP

The climate of India is broadly a tropical monsoon climate. The Indian Meteorological Department divides the year into four seasons — tap them in the order they arrive.

Winter generally lasts from December to early April; December and January are coldest, averaging 10–15 °C in the north-west and rising towards the equator to 20–25 °C in mainland India's south-east. Summer or pre-monsoon spans April to June, or into July in the north-west: April is hottest in the west and south, May in the north, and most of inland India averages 32–40 °C.

The monsoon or advancing monsoon generally runs June to September, dominated by the humid south-west summer monsoon that sweeps across the country in late May or early June. The post-monsoon or retreating monsoon lasts October to December, and in north-western India October and November are usually cloudless. The Himalayan states, being more temperate, experience two additional seasons: autumn and spring.

09The six ṛtusTable 3.2 · the traditional Indian year30 XP

Traditionally India counts six seasons, each about two months long, based on dividing the twelve months astronomically into six parts. Match each to where it falls in the Gregorian year.

Tap a ṛtu, then tap its months.

The traditional Indian calendar reflects these seasons in the arrangement of its months — Chaitra and Vaiśhākha for Vasanta, Śhrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada for Varṣhā, and so on. These seasons and their duration may vary across different parts of the country.

Think about it
Hindustani classical music associates certain rāgas with specific seasons. Find out with your elders and teachers which rāgas are connected to each of the six. And note that Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra already contains records of scientific measurements of rainfall, used in managing the country's revenue and its relief efforts.
10The monsoon engineWhy the wind reverses twice a year35 XP

Land and sea again — but this time over a whole subcontinent and a whole year. Run through the months and watch the wind turn right around.

Warmer
—
Wind
—
Rain
—

The word comes from the Arabic mausim, meaning season: Arab traders named the seasonal reversal of the wind system, and the sailors who reached India in ancient times were among the first to notice it, since they travelled at the mercy of the winds. A monsoon is a seasonal reversal in wind direction during a year.

The south-west or summer monsoon blows from sea to land across the Indian Ocean, the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal between June and September. It is caused by the unequal heating of land and sea: in summer the landmass of India heats faster than the surrounding oceans, creating low pressure over the subcontinent while the cooler Indian Ocean holds high pressure. Winds move from high to low, so moist air blows in off the ocean and brings rain — most of the country's rainfall for the whole year.

The north-east or winter monsoon runs from October to February. Now the land cools faster than the oceans, so high pressure sits over the land and low over the seas, and cold dry winds blow from land to sea. They bring no rain to most of India — but where they cross the Bay of Bengal they pick up moisture and rain on the eastern coast, especially Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka.

Don't miss out
Because crops depended on the rains, Indians worked out ways to predict them. The Kṛiṣhiparāśhara based its main technique on the positions of the Moon and the Sun; Varāhamihira's Bṛihatsaṁhitā used the lunar mansions, or nakṣhatras — 27 equal divisions of the sky along the Moon's path, one for roughly each night of its circuit. A great many farming practices in India still rest on these methods. Kālidāsa, in the Meghadūtam of about the 5th century CE, even gives the date the monsoon breaks over central India and traces the path its clouds take.

The rain does not arrive everywhere at once. Drag the date from late May to late October and watch it cross the country and then back out again.

Phase
—
Under monsoon
—

—

Monsoon rain begins to recede from north India at the beginning of October, and South India typically receives more rainfall during that time. The whole cycle takes about seven weeks to cover the country and another four to leave it.

Monsoon plays a vital role in the lives of people in India. Most of the country's agriculture depends on it, as farmers rely on the rain for sowing and growing. A good monsoon ensures sufficient food production and water in rivers, reservoirs and wells. It also affects daily life, transport, festivals and employment, especially in rural areas. Excessive rainfall can cause floods, while a weak monsoon can lead to drought — so the monsoon shapes the economy, the lifestyle and the livelihoods of the country.

Don't miss out
Under the National Monsoon Mission, the Ministry of Earth Sciences has developed state-of-the-art weather and climate prediction models, with the object of improving monsoon prediction for India over every time frame. Mission Mausam aims to make the nation Weather Ready and Climate Smart, with timely and precise observation, modelling and forecasting for agriculture, disaster management and rural development.
Part 4 · A climate that is changing
12Cause, effect, or something we can doSorting out climate change30 XP

Climate change gets discussed as one undifferentiated worry. It is actually three separate lists. Put each item on the right one.

Climate change refers to long-term changes in weather patterns — temperature, rainfall and wind — caused mainly by human activities: the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrial pollution that releases gases such as carbon dioxide. These raise the level of greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour — which trap heat and lift global temperatures.

The results are already visible: more frequent floods and droughts, melting glaciers, rising sea levels and loss of biodiversity. It threatens ecosystems, and it reaches human health, agriculture and livelihoods, with a heavy impact on almost every section of the population, women and children included. Tackling it takes collective effort — reducing carbon footprints, using renewable energy, protecting forests and adopting sustainable lifestyles.

A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere as a result of human activities — energy use, transportation, and the production of goods and services. Low-impact choices score 1 point, medium 2, high 3 and very high 4, so a lower total is the better one.

The point of the exercise is the last step, not the number. Think of two simple changes you could make to reduce your score, and write them down as a climate action pledge. Every small step counts.

14Punjab 2025: what actually caused itA case study, split in two30 XP

In 2025 Punjab flooded badly. The chapter separates what nature did from what people had done first. Sort each cause.

In 2025 Punjab experienced severe floods after very heavy monsoon rain and the consecutive swelling of the Satluj, Beas and Ravi. Villages, farmland, houses and infrastructure such as roads and bridges were damaged across large parts of the state. Even as water receded in places and relief operations ran, the overall impact was devastating: heavy economic losses, social disruption and environmental damage.

Many people lost their lives, and thousands had to leave home for relief camps. Large areas of farmland went under water and crops such as paddy were severely damaged. Poultry and dairy farms were destroyed and many animals sickened or died. Roads, bridges, border fences and public buildings were damaged, and murky standing water spread waterborne disease and sanitation problems.

Classroom discussion
To what extent did natural factors cause these floods compared with human activities? Could better planning have reduced the damage, and how? What are the National Disaster Management Authority's guidelines for flood management? And what part can students and young people play in disaster preparedness?

Compare Shillong with Kolkata, and Delhi with Jodhpur, and the reason for the difference is relief and distance from the sea. Look at Thiruvananthapuram and you find an equable climate — the sea will not let it get very hot or very cold. Look at Chennai and the rain arrives only once the monsoon has finished almost everywhere else, because it depends on the retreating north-east monsoon crossing the Bay of Bengal. Look at Leh and there is barely any rain at all.

Despite all these differences, one thing runs through every station on the list: the year is organised around the monsoon. That is the framework that lends climatic unity to the whole country.
